definition: Persuasive means able to win others over to believe or do something, as a well-crafted argument, speech, or appeal does.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word persuasive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know persuasive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Maya's persuasive presentation on cafeteria composting won over even the skeptical head custodian by the final slide.
A plausible claim merely seems believable; a persuasive one actually moves people to agree or act.
A compelling argument is stronger than a persuasive one — it grips its audience so firmly that resisting it feels nearly impossible.

Convincing is what evidence and proof are when they remove doubt — a convincing alibi, convincing data. Persuasive belongs to appeals crafted to move people: speeches, ads, essays. The security footage is convincing though it argues nothing; the closing speech is persuasive because it was built to win you over.

Influential describes broad power to shape opinion over time — an influential critic, an influential study whose ideas spread for years. Persuasive works close up: one argument moving one audience toward one belief or decision. An influential thinker shapes a field; a persuasive presentation wins Tuesday's vote.

Effective says only that something achieves its purpose, whatever the purpose is — an effective medicine, an effective filing system. Persuasive names one specific effect: changing what people believe or do. A door lock can be effective; only something that moves minds is persuasive.
An unconvincing case leaves its audience exactly where it found them.

Persuasive means able to win others over to believe or do something, as a well-crafted argument, speech, or appeal does.
The documentary about the town's overflowing landfill was so persuasive that, within a year, weekend recycling drop-offs had tripled.
The film actually changed what people did—tripling recycling—which is the test for persuasive: it convinces others to believe or act.
A speech can be full of clever technique, but it only earns the word persuasive if it genuinely moves its audience.
Persuasive is judged by results: a persuasive essay, ad, or friend actually moves people to agree or act.
It pairs naturally with the arguments you write in school.
Unlike rhetorical, which points at technique, persuasive points at effect—did any minds actually change?

When the county proposed closing the library on Sundays, head librarian Ruth Okafor asked for ten minutes at the budget hearing.
She did not bring spreadsheets.
She brought three stories: a night-shift nurse who studies for her licensing exam on Sunday afternoons, a father who reads aloud to twins there, a teenager who discovered chess at the Sunday club.
Each story ended the same way, with the door she asked the board to keep open.
Reporters later called the speech the most persuasive thing said all evening — not because it proved anything, but because it was built, story by story, to move nine votes.
The Sunday hours survived by two.
